Excess mortality

Source: R/derive-excess.R
mt_excess.Rd

Excess deaths are the observed deaths minus the deaths expected without the shock, from a baseline model fitted to the years before it, given the observed exposures of the later years. The WHO estimates of the excess mortality of the COVID-19 pandemic also compare observed deaths with expected deaths from a baseline model (Msemburi et al. 2023); Acosta and Irizarry (2022) describe a model of the excess itself.

Usage

mt_excess(
  model,
  data,
  baseline = NULL,
  periods = NULL,
  quantity = c("deaths", "life_expectancy"),
  by = NULL,
  ages = NULL,
  cumulative = FALSE,
  at = NULL,
  n_draws = 500,
  seed = NULL,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975),
  include_estimated = FALSE,
  prep = NULL,
  ...
)

mt_plot_excess(
  x,
  type = c("expected", "excess", "p_score"),
  level = 0.95,
  colour = NULL
)

Arguments

model

An mt_fit of the baseline model, fitted to the years before the shock, or a model specification, which is then fitted to the baseline years of data.

data

An mt_data object with the observed deaths and exposures of the years of interest (it may also contain the baseline years).

baseline

For a model specification: the first and last year of the baseline (c(1990, 2002)).

periods

Years for which the excess is estimated (default: every year of data after the baseline).

quantity

"deaths" or "life_expectancy".

by

Stratum variables kept in the result (default all, one row per stratum); the deaths of strata with the same values of by are summed. character() sums all strata. Strata at the total or group levels of a hierarchy (see mt_aggregate_strata()) are left out of the sums over their variable.

ages

Age groups of the result: NULL sums over all ages, a numeric vector gives the start of each group (c(0, 65, 85): 0-64, 65-84 and 85+; ages below the first value are left out), and "observed" keeps the age groups of the observed deaths. Observed cells must lie within the groups. Deaths only.

cumulative

Sum over the years of periods up to each year (deaths only). Column from gives the first year of the sum.

at

Age for life expectancy (default the first age).

n_draws

Number of draws of the expected deaths.

seed

Random seed of the forecast draws (NULL leaves the random number generator as is).

probs

Quantile levels.

include_estimated

Use cells whose deaths were estimated.

prep

Preprocessing pipeline (mt_prep()) for a model specification.

...

Passed to the life-table calculation for life expectancy (ax, open, k).

x

An mt_excess() result.

type

"expected" (observed and expected values), "excess" or "p_score".

level

Level of the interval shown (its quantiles must be in x).

colour

Stratum variable that gives the colours (default: the one with the most levels).

Value

mt_excess(): a data.table with the by variables, age, age_lo and age_hi (deaths), period, observed, the mean and quantiles of expected and excess (expected_mean, expected_q0.025, ...), for deaths those of p_score (from the mean and quantiles of the expected deaths), then p_positive, cells and skipped; for life expectancy also at. mt_plot_excess(): a ggplot object.

Details

The estimand: here the expected deaths are draws of mt_forecast() with predictive = TRUE, that is draws from the predictive distribution of the deaths under the baseline model (the uncertainty of the baseline trend plus the Poisson variation of the death counts given the rates; negative binomial for stanmomo(family = "nb")). They describe the counterfactual deaths: the deaths that would have been observed without the shock. The observed deaths minus each draw give draws of the excess, so its interval is a prediction interval for the realised excess, the observed minus the realised counterfactual deaths, not a confidence interval for an expected excess. It has its nominal coverage when the baseline model is correct; an interval that contains zero means deaths within the range of the counterfactual deaths.

The result gives, for each row, the observed deaths and the mean and quantiles of

  • expected: the expected (counterfactual) deaths;

  • excess: observed minus expected deaths, draw by draw;

  • p_score: the excess in percent of the expected deaths, 100 * (observed / expected - 1). Its quantiles are those of the expected deaths transformed (the P-score at level p is 100 * (observed / q - 1) with q the quantile of the expected deaths at level 1 - p, since the P-score decreases as the expected deaths increase), and p_score_mean is the P-score of the mean expected deaths, so a draw without expected deaths (small cells) does not make the row missing;

and p_positive, the share of draws with a positive excess: the predictive probability that the observed deaths (or life expectancy) exceed the counterfactual ones under the baseline model. 1 - p_positive is a one-sided predictive p-value for the hypothesis of no excess.

Sums over ages (ages), strata (by) and years (cumulative) are formed draw by draw before the quantiles are taken. With quantity = "life_expectancy", the excess is the observed life expectancy at age at minus that of each draw of expected deaths, so a loss of life expectancy is negative; strata are combined by summing their deaths and exposures.

The deaths are compared at their observed resolution: the draws on the grid of the model are summed to each observed cell, so a model fitted on single years of age (for example with prep = mt_prep(step_ungroup())) can be compared with deaths in 5-year groups. As in mt_backtest(), cells whose deaths were estimated (provenance "estimated", for example suppressed cells filled by mt_fill_suppressed()) and missing cells are left out unless include_estimated = TRUE; columns cells and skipped count the cells used and left out. For life expectancy, years with a cell left out are skipped with a warning.

The baseline should end with the last year before the shock and leave out years of other shocks (wars, earlier epidemics). Models need consecutive years, so the baseline is one span of years. The expected deaths of a long gap between the baseline and the shock (for example 1914-1917 for 1918 with a baseline 1900-1913) are forecasts over the whole gap, with correspondingly wide intervals.

mt_plot_excess() draws the result: observed and expected values over the years (type = "expected"), or the excess or P-score with its interval by age group (when there are several) or year. For one year and one age group, each level of the colour variable (for example each region) gets its own row.

References

Acosta RJ, Irizarry RA (2022). A flexible statistical framework for estimating excess mortality. Epidemiology 33(3): 346-353. doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001445

Msemburi W, Karlinsky A, Knutson V, Aleshin-Guendel S, Chatterji S, Wakefield J (2023). The WHO estimates of excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. Nature 613: 130-137. doi:10.1038/s41586-022-05522-2

Examples

x <- mt_example(years = 2000:2019, deaths = "single")
# a shock: 10% more deaths at ages 70+ in 2018 and 2019
x$obs$deaths[period_lo >= 2018 & age_lo >= 70, value := round(1.1 * value)]
#>       stratum age_lo age_hi period_lo period_hi value provenance
#>         <int>  <num>  <num>     <num>     <num> <num>     <char>
#>    1:       1     30     31      2000      2001    53   observed
#>    2:       1     31     32      2000      2001    57   observed
#>    3:       1     32     33      2000      2001    58   observed
#>    4:       1     33     34      2000      2001    57   observed
#>    5:       1     34     35      2000      2001    47   observed
#>   ---                                                           
#> 2836:       2     96     97      2019      2020  1301   observed
#> 2837:       2     97     98      2019      2020  1042   observed
#> 2838:       2     98     99      2019      2020   721   observed
#> 2839:       2     99    100      2019      2020   559   observed
#> 2840:       2    100    Inf      2019      2020   890   observed
ex <- mt_excess(lee_carter(), x, baseline = c(2000, 2015), ages = c(30, 70),
                n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
ex[, list(sex, age, period, observed, excess_q0.5, p_score_q0.025, p_score_q0.975)]
#>        sex    age period observed excess_q0.5 p_score_q0.025 p_score_q0.975
